extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, research-integrity professionals, and readers interested in scholarly publishing and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and characterizing forms of research-publication problems (errors, ethical breaches, and signs of paper-mill activity) that lead to corrections, retractions, delisting, or investigations. The page is a news roundup documenting specific incidents and the behaviors or indicators that prompted editorial or indexing actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant and accurate citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cited references must be relevant to the claims they are meant to support; irrelevant citations can be grounds for retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from the page: a 2024 article was retracted after publishers discovered 'five of the cited references weren’t relevant to the claims they were meant to be supporting.' Irrelevant or misleading citations that materially affect the support for claims are treated as serious faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and support for figures/flow diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Information presented in figures or flow diagrams must be supported elsewhere in the article (text, methods, or data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors flagged that 'information in a flow diagram for selecting studies didn’t appear anywhere else in the article.' Discrepancies between diagrams and the article body are problematic and can contribute to retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized authorship changes and valid contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Any change to author lists during revision must have editorial approval; providing fictitious or false contact information during submission is unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page reports papers where 'authors changed without editorial approval during revision of the manuscripts' and where 'authors also provided fictitious email addresses during the submission process.' Such actions can lead to retraction because they undermine the integrity of the submission and review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-institutional emails and other paper‑mill signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of non-institutional email addresses or other markers (e.g., listings of 'articles ready for acceptance') can be indicators of paper-mill involvement and warrant additional scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that non-institutional emails 'can be signs of paper-mill involvement' and cites a website that listed 'articles ready for acceptance' as an example of suspicious external evidence prompting journal action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image/data duplication or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Identical or duplicated images/plots presented as representing different experiments/systems constitute image duplication or fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: retraction notices cited 'identical plots supposedly representing different chemical systems.' Duplicate or manipulated images that misrepresent results are common grounds for retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-citation manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificially increasing self-citations (e.g., self-citations multiplying between submission and publication) is a form of manipulation and may be considered misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page describes papers where 'self-citations multiplying between manuscript submission and publication' were noted in retraction notices as problematic behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromised peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the peer-review process was compromised (manipulated reviewers, fake reviews, or other irregularities) undermines trust in publication and can lead to retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices referenced 'compromised peer review' as a reason for pulling papers. Journals investigate and retract when review integrity cannot be substantiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental methodological or analytical errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious errors in analysis or methods that invalidate findings are grounds for correction or retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'fundamental errors in chemical analyses' cited in retraction notices — errors that render results unreliable justify editorial action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresentation of institutional affiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorrectly stating or misrepresenting an institutional affiliation (claiming association when none exists) is misconduct and can prompt retraction or correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices stated 'the research described in the article is not associated with that institution' and that an 'affiliation was given incorrectly.' Misstated affiliations are taken seriously by journals and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial conflict of interest (editors publishing in their own journals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors who oversee review of manuscripts and then make the final decision to publish their own work or work they edited face conflicts of interest; lack of proper safeguards can lead to retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page reports a case where a finance professor 'oversaw the review of the articles and made "the final decision" to publish them in three journals he edited' and where that process was questioned by the publisher and led to retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ghostwriting and undisclosed contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to disclose ghostwriting (e.g., company employees writing a paper without being named) or undisclosed substantial contributors is a breach of authorship and disclosure norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The site recounts a review article retracted after documents revealed Monsanto employees ghostwrote the article but were 'not named as coauthors.' Ghostwriting can lead to retraction even years later when revealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to disclose conflicts of interest (COI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must disclose relevant financial or other conflicts of interest; nondisclosure can undermine trust and be cause for correction or retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page includes posts categorized under 'failure to disclose COI' (e.g., the glyphosate article example), illustrating that undisclosed COIs are a key criterion for editorial action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in funding statements and correction practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding statements must be accurate and any post-publication changes should be handled transparently with formal corrections or notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes an incident where a journal 'quietly removed part of a funding statement ... without issuing correction,' which experts called 'worrying.' Proper practice is to issue transparent corrections if funding disclosures change or were wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coercive citation and citation manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Coercing authors to cite a journal's articles or other forms of citation manipulation are considered unethical and can lead to delisting or other sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a journal was flagged after allegations it was 'coercing authors to cite its articles.' Citation manipulation was cited as a reason for re-evaluation and indexing actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing and quality-control criteria (Clarivate/Scopus actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexing services monitor journal quality and can place titles 'on hold' or delist them for concerns such as outlier publication performance or quality issues; journals must remedy issues and backfill missing content to regain standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarivate put a journal on hold for 'concerns about the quality of the content.' The 'on-hold' status prevents new content from being indexed; Clarivate requires a journal to be taken off hold and have missing content backfilled by a deadline (e.g., August 1) to receive an impact factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: High publication volume with elevated retraction rates as a red flag
rubrics_metrics.description: Extremely high output combined with a high number or rate of retractions suggests systemic editorial/quality-control problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mega-journal Heliyon published tens of thousands of papers (e.g., 'over 11,000 papers in 2023 and more than 17,000 in 2024') while issuing hundreds of retractions, prompting an internal audit and wider scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction triggers summary (errors, ethics, and manipulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions are commonly triggered by a range of issues including irrelevant citations, figure inconsistencies, authorship irregularities, image duplication, compromised review, ghostwriting, COI failures, and citation manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Across multiple cases reported on the page, retraction notices list combinations of the above issues. The aggregate guidance: journals and publishers treat these problems as sufficient cause for correction, investigation, or retraction depending on severity.
